prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place the GLP-1 achievement first, and the scientific case supports that. It is a continuous chain from gut-hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and action in humans, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology and the therapeutic rationale, Mojsov on the active GLP-1 peptide form) to a drug class with large randomised outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease. It is mature, independently confirmed and clearly a discovery in physiology and medicine, not only a drug-development story. After reading colleagues' arguments I move from my opening trio (which included Knudsen) to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, because a physiology-and-medicine citation is best anchored on the discovery of the hormone's action and its active form.
statement.case_against: Credit is the real weakness. Early GLP-1 work outside the supplied names (for example Habener's group) has claims, the Mojsov priority question is disputed, and a three-person limit leaves out Knudsen, whose acylated analogues (liraglutide, semaglutide) are what made the biology usable at scale. A prize that omits the drug design may look incomplete, and one that includes it risks rewarding industrial development over discovery. Unanimous opening support also says little about whether this credit split would survive scrutiny.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for GLP-1 and leaves out Knudsen as pharmaceutical development; also ranks optogenetics (B049) fourth with Bamberg, Nagel and Deisseroth.
responses.response: I now agree on the GLP-1 trio, having proposed Knudsen myself at opening. The discovery logic is stronger with Mojsov than with the drug design, and I would handle Knudsen's contribution in the citation wording rather than by name. I am less persuaded on optogenetics: the channelrhodopsin discovery and its neuronal deployment involve at least six credible people, and any choice of three, yours included, leaves out Hegemann or Boyden. I would not advance B049 until that attribution can be defended.

responses.point: Prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for GLP-1, treating Mojsov's contribution as contested, and ranks optogenetics third and cGAS-STING fifth.
responses.response: My opening matched your trio, so I take the Knudsen argument seriously: without long-acting analogues the physiology would not have become a therapy. But the priority dispute over the active peptide is a question of who identified what, and excluding Mojsov would be harder to defend than excluding a drug-design contribution within a physiology prize. On cGAS-STING I agree the mechanism is clear and original, but the clinical payoff is unproven and the STING credit (Barber, Ishikawa, Sun, Wu) is unsettled, so I would hold it for a later year.

responses.point: Ranks GLP-1 first and CAR-T second, with imatinib (B024) third, and notes that Eshhar's omission weakens the CAR-T trio and that Rosenberg's role may be a separate adoptive-transfer discovery.
responses.response: I share your concern on CAR-T. I put June, Sadelain and Rosenberg together at opening, but the missing originator of the chimeric receptor concept and Rosenberg's distinct lineage mean this configuration is not clean, which is why I keep it as an alternative and not as a second prize part. I also see imatinib as a strong, very mature achievement, but it is largely drug development resting on earlier, separately recognised work on the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL. I rank it below the anti-TNF line, though I accept that is a judgment about weighting.

responses.point: Ranks GLP-1 first, then imatinib and HPV VLP vaccines as the next strongest, and flags priority and patent complexity for HPV (Frazer and Zhou) and prior recognition of zur Hausen.
responses.response: I agree HPV VLP vaccines are an unusual case of demonstrated population-level cancer prevention. My reservation is the priority complexity you name: with Frazer and Zhou contested and the 2008 prize covering the HPV-cancer link, I do not see a defensible trio yet. I would place it behind CAR-T and anti-TNF, but I do not think the committee should dismiss it.

responses.point: Proposes a two-person CAR-T configuration (June and Sadelain) and ranks TNF blockade (B018) low, querying whether it is mostly clinical translation.
responses.response: I agree that dropping Rosenberg gives a cleaner CAR-T pair. On anti-TNF, I would not call it only clinical translation. Feldmann and Maini showed in human synovium that TNF drives the cytokine cascade and then proved that blocking it works, which established anti-cytokine therapy across several diseases. The competing claims (Kollias, Cerami, Vilcek, and the antibody engineers) are real, and that is why it is an alternative of mine and not my lead.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1 peptide can be credited without displacing Habener-type early contributors or Knudsen's drug design.
Whether the committee wants a physiology-centred citation or one that explicitly covers therapeutic development.
If GLP-1 is settled, whether a second distinct part (CAR-T or anti-TNF) is worth the attribution cost under the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My field is autoimmunity and rheumatology, which touches anti-TNF therapy (B018, an alternative) and CAR-T in autoimmune disease, but my profile documents no collaboration with any credited candidate, so I flag only the topical proximity.
